notes: A forest shrine in central Tokyo planted with some 100,000 donated trees.

details.history: Established in 1920 to enshrine the spirits of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set within an artificial evergreen forest designed to mature over centuries.
details.why_visit: One of Japan's most visited shrines, drawing millions for hatsumode, and a tranquil expanse of woodland minutes from Harajuku.
details.prayer_focus: Family harmony (家内安全), peace of the nation, and the fulfillment of heartfelt wishes, often written on ema beneath the great camphor trees.
details.best_season: New Year for hatsumode; fresh green in early summer; the November autumn festival.

deities.role: Enshrined sovereign (主祭神) of the Meiji era.
deities.regional_lore: Enshrined here together with his consort in 1920, eight years after his death, by national subscription; the surrounding forest was raised from saplings donated from every province of Japan and the colonies.

canonical.domain: Imperial rule and the modernization of Japan
canonical.title: 122nd Emperor of Japan (1852–1912)
canonical.canonical_lore: The emperor under whom Japan transformed from a feudal society into a modern state during the Meiji Restoration.

canonical.title: Empress consort of Emperor Meiji (1849–1914)
canonical.canonical_lore: Remembered for her patronage of women's education and of the Red Cross in Japan.

events.time_prose: Late April to early May, around the Showa Day holiday.
events.origin: An annual rite honoring the enshrined spirits, paired with public performances of classical arts.
events.meaning: Thanksgiving and prayer for the peace and prosperity of the nation.
events.ritual: Court music (gagaku), bugaku dance, noh, and yabusame horseback archery are offered before the deities.
events.prayer: For national peace and the people's wellbeing.
events.visitor_notes: The traditional-arts offerings are free to watch on the festival grounds.

sources.title: 明治神宮 公式サイト
sources.note: Enshrined deities, grounds, and annual rites.
